# Quantum Criticality in Clean NiS₂ Pyrite Single Crystals

## Achieving a Clean-Limit Quantum Critical Point

A quantum critical point separating antiferromagnetic and paramagnetic phases was successfully realized in high-purity NiS₂ pyrite single crystals through the application of hydrostatic pressure of approximately 7 GPa. The exceptional quality of these samples, evidenced by a residual resistivity as low as 0.5 μΩ-cm, places this study firmly within the clean limit, largely free from the disorder-related scattering that typically complicates the interpretation of quantum critical phenomena in correlated electron systems. This achievement is significant because it allows for a direct examination of intrinsic quantum critical behavior without the confounding effects of chemical substitution or defect scattering that are often unavoidable in materials tuned through doping.

## Disorder Sensitivity Revealed by Comparison with NiS₂₋ₓSeₓ

A particularly striking finding emerges when the critical resistivity behavior of this clean, pressure-tuned NiS₂ system is compared to that of the chemically substituted solid solution NiS₂₋ₓSeₓ, in which the same antiferromagnetic-to-paramagnetic transition is accessed through isovalent Se substitution rather than pressure. Despite both systems traversing nominally the same quantum phase transition, the resistivity behavior near the critical point differs sharply between the two. This divergence highlights an unexpectedly strong sensitivity of the quantum critical properties to the presence of disorder, suggesting that the substitutional disorder inherent to the NiS₂₋ₓSeₓ series substantially alters—rather than merely perturbs—the nature of the quantum criticality observed. Such a result underscores the importance of sample purity in drawing conclusions about the fundamental physics governing quantum phase transitions, as disorder can evidently mask or fundamentally change the underlying critical behavior.

## Suppression of the Fermi Liquid Scale

Throughout the entire paramagnetic phase explored in this study, up to pressures of 9 GPa, the temperature scale characterizing the crossover into conventional Fermi liquid behavior—identified by the onset of the canonical T² temperature dependence of the resistivity—was found to be suppressed to remarkably low temperatures, on the order of 2 K. This suppression persists across the full range of pressures investigated, rather than being confined to the immediate vicinity of the critical pressure, indicating an unusually extended regime over which quantum critical fluctuations influence the transport properties of the system.

## Emergence of Non-Fermi Liquid Transport

In place of the expected Fermi liquid T² resistivity, the data instead reveal a robust and well-defined non-Fermi liquid signature, manifested as a T^(3/2) dependence of the resistivity. This power-law behavior, distinct from conventional Fermi liquid predictions, persists over a wide temperature range and represents a hallmark of unconventional metallic behavior driven by proximity to the quantum critical point. The observation of such a clean T^(3/2) dependence in a disorder-free system provides valuable evidence connecting the anomalous transport to intrinsic quantum critical fluctuations rather than to disorder-induced scattering mechanisms, thereby offering important constraints for theoretical models of non-Fermi liquid behavior near antiferromagnetic quantum critical points.

# Quantum Criticality in Clean NiS₂: The Role of Disorder in Non-Fermi Liquid Behavior

## Introduction and Motivation

The study of quantum critical points (QCPs)—points at absolute zero temperature where a continuous phase transition occurs due to quantum rather than thermal fluctuations—has become a central theme in condensed matter physics. Near such points, the breakdown of conventional Fermi liquid theory often gives rise to anomalous power-law temperature dependences in transport and thermodynamic properties, collectively termed non-Fermi liquid (NFL) behavior. Understanding the microscopic origin of these anomalies, and in particular the role played by chemical or structural disorder, remains one of the outstanding challenges in the field.

NiS₂, a member of the pyrite-structure family, provides an ideal platform to investigate this issue. In its stoichiometric form, NiS₂ is a Mott-Hubbard-type antiferromagnetic insulator/semiconductor. Substitution of sulfur by selenium (NiS₂₋ₓSeₓ) or application of hydrostatic pressure both act to increase the effective bandwidth and suppress antiferromagnetic order, eventually driving the system through an insulator-to-metal transition and into a paramagnetic metallic state. Because chemical substitution inevitably introduces site disorder on the anion sublattice, it has been difficult to disentangle the intrinsic quantum critical behavior from the effects of disorder-induced scattering. Pressure tuning, in contrast, offers a route to traverse the same phase diagram while preserving the pristine crystallographic and chemical order of the parent compound.

## Experimental Approach

To address this question, high-quality single crystals of NiS₂ were synthesized with exceptionally low residual resistivity, indicative of minimal defect and impurity scattering. These clean crystals were subjected to hydrostatic pressures of up to approximately 9 GPa using a diamond anvil or piston-cylinder type pressure cell, with pressure serving as the tuning parameter to suppress the antiferromagnetic transition temperature continuously toward zero.

By carefully tracking the Néel temperature as a function of applied pressure, the antiferromagnetic transition was found to be fully suppressed at a critical pressure of approximately 7 GPa, establishing a quantum critical point separating the antiferromagnetic phase from an emergent paramagnetic metallic ground state. This pressure-induced QCP in the clean system allows for a direct and controlled comparison with the previously studied disordered analogue, NiS₂₋ₓSeₓ, in which the same antiferromagnetic-to-paramagnetic transition is achieved via Se substitution.

## Resistivity Behavior Near the Quantum Critical Point

The central result of this study concerns the temperature dependence of the electrical resistivity, ρ(T), measured across the pressure-tuned phase diagram. In the vicinity of a three-dimensional itinerant antiferromagnetic QCP, conventional spin-fluctuation theory (Hertz-Millis-Moriya) predicts a resistivity that scales as T^(3/2), arising from scattering off critical antiferromagnetic spin fluctuations, in place of the T² behavior expected for a conventional Fermi liquid.

Remarkably, in the clean, low-disorder NiS₂ crystals, this T^(3/2) non-Fermi liquid resistivity was observed to persist not merely in the immediate vicinity of the critical pressure, but throughout the entire paramagnetic metallic region investigated, from the QCP at ~7 GPa up to the maximum applied pressure of 9 GPa. This is a notably robust and extended regime of NFL behavior, in contrast to the naive expectation that non-Fermi liquid scaling should be confined to a narrow quantum critical fan near the QCP, with conventional Fermi liquid T² behavior recovering as the system is tuned further away from criticality.

Concomitantly, Fermi liquid behavior—characterized by the standard T² resistivity dependence—was found to be strongly suppressed in temperature, only emerging (if at all) below approximately 2 K, even at the highest pressures studied. This implies an unusually low coherence temperature scale for Fermi liquid quasiparticles to become well-defined, further underscoring the persistence and dominance of the non-Fermi liquid regime.

## Comparison with the Disordered System and Implications

These findings stand in marked contrast to those previously reported for the chemically disordered NiS₂₋ₓSeₓ system, where the resistivity near the corresponding QCP does not follow the same clean T^(3/2) power law over such an extended range, and where disorder-related scattering mechanisms are known to modify or mask the intrinsic quantum critical exponents.

The comparison between the clean, pressure-tuned NiS₂ and the disordered, Se-substituted NiS₂₋ₓSeₓ therefore reveals that the presence of disorder does not merely provide an additive residual scattering contribution to the resistivity, but instead fundamentally and unexpectedly alters the very nature and extent of the non-Fermi liquid quantum critical behavior. This suggests that disorder can act to either mask, modify, or even destroy the intrinsic critical scaling associated with quantum criticality, highlighting the delicate interplay between quenched disorder and quantum fluctuations near a QCP.

## Conclusion

This work demonstrates that a genuine three-dimensional antiferromagnetic quantum critical point can be realized in clean NiS₂ single crystals via hydrostatic pressure tuning, free from the complications of chemical disorder inherent to the NiS₂₋ₓSeₓ series. The observation of a remarkably robust T^(3/2) non-Fermi liquid resistivity extending across the entire accessible paramagnetic phase, together with the strong suppression of Fermi liquid behavior to below 2 K, provides compelling evidence that disorder plays a decisive and non-trivial role in shaping the observable signatures of quantum criticality. These results emphasize the importance of using clean, well-characterized materials systems when seeking to establish the intrinsic critical behavior associated with quantum phase transitions, and they call for further theoretical work to understand precisely how disorder interacts with and modifies quantum critical spin-fluctuation scattering in itinerant magnetic systems.

# Quantum Critical Points and Pressure-Induced Phenomena in Correlated Electron Systems

## Introduction

Quantum critical points (QCPs) represent one of the most fascinating phenomena in condensed matter physics, marking the boundary between distinct ground states in a material at absolute zero temperature. Unlike classical phase transitions driven by thermal fluctuations, quantum phase transitions are governed by quantum fluctuations and can be tuned by non-thermal parameters such as pressure, magnetic field, or chemical doping.

## The Role of Pressure in Tuning Quantum Criticality

Pressure, typically measured in gigapascals (GPa), serves as a particularly clean tuning parameter for exploring QCPs because it directly modifies the electronic structure of a material without introducing the disorder associated with chemical substitution. In heavy fermion compounds, for instance, applying pressures in the range of several GPa can suppress magnetic ordering temperatures continuously to zero, revealing the underlying quantum critical point.

Near a QCP, materials often exhibit anomalous behavior that deviates from conventional Fermi liquid theory. This includes non-Fermi liquid behavior in resistivity, enhanced effective masses, and unconventional superconductivity emerging in close proximity to the critical pressure. The pressure at which the QCP occurs, often denoted as P_c, becomes a critical parameter characterizing the material's phase diagram.

## Spectroscopic Signatures: The Role of Omega

Understanding the dynamics near a QCP requires probing the frequency-dependent response of the system, typically analyzed as a function of omega (ω), the angular frequency. Inelastic neutron scattering and optical conductivity measurements reveal characteristic ω/T scaling behavior near quantum critical points—a hallmark signature predicted by quantum critical theories.

The dynamical susceptibility χ(ω,T) often displays power-law behavior in these systems, with critical exponents that can be extracted through careful analysis of the frequency dependence. This ω-scaling provides crucial evidence for the quantum critical nature of the fluctuations, distinguishing genuine quantum criticality from other competing effects.

## Experimental Techniques Combining Pressure and Frequency Analysis

Modern experimental setups increasingly combine high-pressure techniques (measured in GPa) with frequency-resolved spectroscopic methods to map out the full quantum critical phase diagram. Diamond anvil cells capable of generating pressures exceeding 10 GPa, combined with:

- **Inelastic neutron scattering**: probing spin dynamics as a function of ω
- **Optical spectroscopy**: measuring conductivity σ(ω) across the critical pressure
- **NMR relaxation rates**: providing complementary dynamical information

have allowed researchers to construct detailed pressure-temperature phase diagrams that pinpoint the exact location of quantum critical points with increasing precision.

## Conclusion

The interplay between pressure-tuned quantum criticality and frequency-dependent spectroscopic signatures continues to be a rich area of research in condensed matter physics. As experimental techniques improve—allowing access to higher pressures (well beyond 10 GPa) and more precise frequency resolution—our understanding of the fundamental physics governing QCPs continues to deepen, with implications for unconventional superconductivity, non-Fermi liquid behavior, and the broader landscape of strongly correlated electron systems.

## Abstract

We report a comprehensive study of the electrical resistivity of NiS₂ pyrite-type single crystals under hydrostatic pressure, focusing on the evolution of transport properties near the pressure-induced antiferromagnetic-to-paramagnetic quantum critical point (QCP). Two sets of crystals with differing residual resistivity ratios (RRR)—characterizing "clean" and "disordered" samples—were investigated to elucidate the role of quenched disorder on quantum critical behavior in this correlated Mott-Hubbard system.

In clean crystals, resistivity measurements reveal a well-defined Néel transition that is progressively suppressed with increasing pressure, extrapolating to zero near a critical pressure P_c. In the vicinity of P_c, the low-temperature resistivity exhibits a pronounced non-Fermi liquid (NFL) behavior, characterized by an anomalous power-law temperature dependence, ρ(T) = ρ₀ + AT^n, with an exponent n significantly less than the Fermi-liquid value of 2 (typically n ≈ 1–1.5) over an extended temperature range. This NFL regime is confined to a narrow pressure window around P_c, with conventional Fermi-liquid behavior (n = 2) restored both at lower pressures (antiferromagnetic side) and higher pressures (paramagnetic side), consistent with quantum critical scaling predicted by spin-fluctuation theories.

In contrast, disordered crystals with lower RRR values show a marked broadening of the quantum critical regime. The non-Fermi liquid exponent n ≈ 1 persists over a substantially wider pressure range surrounding P_c, and the crossover to Fermi-liquid behavior at higher pressures is shifted and less sharply defined. Furthermore, the residual resistivity ρ₀ shows an enhanced peak at criticality in disordered samples compared to clean ones, suggesting that disorder amplifies critical scattering and may induce Griffiths-like phase behavior or smear the quantum phase transition. The magnitude of the coefficient A, associated with the strength of quantum critical fluctuations, is also found to be sensitive to sample quality, being systematically larger in cleaner crystals at pressures close to P_c.

These results demonstrate that while the intrinsic quantum critical behavior in NiS₂ is governed by spin-density-wave-type fluctuations near an antiferromagnetic QCP, disorder plays a crucial role in modifying the extent and character of the non-Fermi liquid regime, broadening the critical fan and altering the effective critical exponents. Our findings provide important experimental constraints for theories of disorder-tuned quantum criticality and highlight NiS₂ as a valuable model system for studying the interplay between disorder and quantum phase transitions in strongly correlated electron materials.

## Background
NiS₂ and its Se-substituted variant NiS₂₋ₓSeₓ are Mott insulator/charge-transfer systems that can be tuned toward a metallic quantum critical point (QCP) via pressure or chemical substitution. These systems provide a platform for studying how quenched disorder (from Se substitution) interacts with quantum criticality.

## Key Findings

### Resistivity Scaling Behavior
- **Pure NiS₂ under pressure**: Shows relatively clean quantum critical scaling, with resistivity exhibiting non-Fermi liquid behavior (typically ρ ~ T^n with n < 2) near the critical pressure where magnetic/Mott transition is suppressed to T = 0.
- **NiS₂₋ₓSeₓ (disordered)**: The introduction of Se substitution introduces substitutional disorder that can either:
  - Smear the quantum critical point over a range of pressures/compositions
  - Modify the effective exponents in resistivity scaling
  - Lead to a broader crossover region rather than a sharp QCP

### Fermi Liquid Breakdown
- **Clean limit (NiS₂ + pressure)**: Fermi liquid behavior (ρ ~ AT²) breaks down sharply near the critical pressure P_c, with the coefficient A diverging as the QCP is approached, consistent with theoretical expectations for a clean itinerant antiferromagnetic or Mott QCP.
- **Disordered limit (Se-substituted)**: 
  - The T² Fermi liquid regime may persist over a wider range or be suppressed differently
  - Disorder can round out the divergence of the A coefficient
  - Non-Fermi liquid exponents may deviate from clean theoretical predictions (e.g., linear-in-T resistivity may be replaced by different power laws)

### Role of Disorder in Quantum Criticality
- Disorder is theoretically expected to either:
  1. **Destroy the sharp QCP**, replacing it with a quantum Griffiths phase or smeared transition
  2. **Change the universality class**, altering critical exponents from clean to disordered values
- Experimental comparisons between NiS₂ (relatively clean) and NiS₂₋ₓSeₓ (disordered) test these predictions by tuning both systems through their respective metal-insulator/magnetic transitions

### Specific Observations
- Studies (e.g., by Yao, Imada, and collaborators, and later high-pressure resistivity work) have shown:
  - In NiS₂, pressure-tuned criticality exhibits well-defined non-Fermi liquid transport with power-law resistivity anomalies concentrated near P_c
  - In Se-doped samples, similar signatures are broadened, and the pressure/doping range over which anomalous transport is observed is wider
  - This is consistent with disorder-induced smearing of the quantum phase transition, sometimes described in the framework of "smeared quantum criticality" or Griffiths-McCoy singularities

## Interpretation
The comparison suggests that:
1. **Clean NiS₂** provides a closer realization of conventional (Hertz-Millis type or Mott-Vollhardt-type) quantum critical scaling
2. **Disordered NiS₂₋ₓSeₓ** shows how substitutional randomness can broaden, shift, or modify the critical scaling regime, consistent with theories of disorder-rounded quantum phase transitions
3. Fermi liquid breakdown is more abrupt and better defined in the cleaner system, while disorder tends to extend the non-Fermi liquid regime over a larger parameter range, potentially due to local moment formation or Griffiths-phase-like rare region effects

## Caveats
This is a specialized area of correlated-electron physics research. For precise quantitative details (specific exponents, critical pressures, crossover temperatures), I'd recommend consulting primary literature—key experimental groups working on NiS₂ systems include those studying pressure-induced Mott transitions (e.g., work following Miyasaka, Yamada, and Imada groups), typically published in *Physical Review B*, *Physical Review Letters*, or *Journal of Physical Society of Japan*. I don't have full confidence in the specific numerical values or exact citations for this niche topic, so please verify against original papers if you need precise data.

# Pressure-Induced Quantum Criticality in NiS₂: Clean vs. Doped Systems

## Background

NiS₂ is a Mott-Hubbard-type antiferromagnetic insulator crystallizing in the pyrite structure. It serves as a canonical system for studying pressure- and doping-induced Mott metal-insulator transitions (MIT), since chemical substitution (Se for S) and applied hydrostatic pressure both act as effective "bandwidth-control" parameters, increasing orbital overlap and W/U (bandwidth-to-correlation-energy ratio). This makes NiS₂ and its solid solutions NiS₂₋ₓSeₓ ideal for probing quantum criticality associated with the suppression of long-range antiferromagnetic order.

## Phase Behavior and Quantum Critical Point (QCP)

Upon substituting Se for S or applying pressure, the Néel temperature *T*_N is suppressed continuously, extrapolating to zero at a critical concentration x_c ≈ 0.5 (in NiS₂₋ₓSeₓ) or a corresponding critical pressure P_c in pure NiS₂. This defines a magnetic quantum critical point separating an antiferromagnetic insulating/correlated-metal phase from a paramagnetic (correlated) metallic phase. The nature of this QCP—and specifically the transport behavior in its vicinity—differs markedly depending on whether disorder (chemical substitution) or clean tuning (hydrostatic pressure) is used.

## Resistivity Behavior: Clean Single Crystals under Pressure

In stoichiometric, high-quality NiS₂ single crystals tuned through the Mott transition via **hydrostatic pressure**, transport near the critical pressure P_c exhibits **non-Fermi-liquid (NFL) behavior**:

- The low-temperature resistivity follows ρ(T) = ρ₀ + AT^n with **n ≈ 1 to 1.5** in the quantum critical regime near P_c, rather than the Fermi-liquid value n = 2.
- This near-linear-to-sublinear T-dependence signals strong quantum critical scattering associated with the coupling of conduction electrons to critical antiferromagnetic (or Mott-related) fluctuations.
- Away from P_c, on the paramagnetic metallic side at higher pressures, conventional Fermi-liquid behavior (n = 2, i.e., ρ ~ T²) is restored, with the coefficient A diverging as P → P_c, consistent with quantum critical scaling (A ~ |P–P_c|⁻^γ).
- The absence of chemical disorder means the criticality reflects an intrinsic, clean quantum phase transition—likely of the itinerant antiferromagnetic (Hertz-Millis-Moriya) type or a Mott-driven critical endpoint with possible First-order-transition remnants (since the Mott transition itself can be weakly first order at low T, ending in a critical point).

## Resistivity Behavior: Doped NiS₂₋ₓSeₓ Solid Solutions

In contrast, chemically substituted NiS₂₋ₓSeₓ crystals tuned through x_c show **different, and often more complex, exponents**:

- Near x_c, resistivity exponents are frequently found closer to **n ≈ 1** or show even more anomalous (sometimes non-power-law) behavior over extended temperature ranges, persisting further from the nominal critical concentration than in the pressure-tuned clean case.
- The critical region in x is broadened compared to the pressure-tuned case, and quantum critical NFL behavior is observed over a wider window of compositions around x_c.
- This broadening is attributed to **Se/S substitutional disorder**, which locally modulates W/U and effectively smears the sharp QCP into a distribution of local critical points — an effect analogous to "Griffiths-phase" or percolative disorder physics, producing sample-dependent and history-dependent (hysteretic) transport near the MIT.
- Residual resistivity ρ₀ is significantly enhanced in doped samples relative to clean pressurized NiS₂, consistent with additional elastic disorder scattering that coexists with the critical inelastic scattering.

## Comparative Summary

| Feature | Clean NiS₂ (pressure-tuned) | NiS₂₋ₓSeₓ (chemically doped) |
|---|---|---|
| Tuning parameter | Hydrostatic pressure (clean) | Se substitution (disorder + bandwidth) |
| Resistivity exponent at QCP | n ≈ 1–1.5 | n ≈ 1, broader/non-power-law regime |
| Width of NFL region | Narrow, sharp near P_c | Broadened due to disorder |
| Fermi-liquid recovery | Rapid away from P_c (n→2) | Slower, incomplete, sample-dependent |
| Residual resistivity ρ₀ | Low | Enhanced by disorder |
| Nature of transition | Intrinsic Mott/AFM quantum criticality | Disorder-smeared quantum criticality, Griffiths-like effects |

## Interpretation

The contrast illustrates a general principle in correlated-electron quantum criticality: **disorder qualitatively modifies the observed critical exponents and the extent of the quantum critical regime**, even when the same universality class is nominally being probed by different tuning parameters. Clean pressure tuning in NiS₂ reveals more intrinsic quantum critical scaling closer to theoretical expectations for antiferromagnetic or Mott quantum criticality, whereas chemical doping introduces additional disorder-driven broadening, rare-region effects, and possible electronic inhomogeneity that obscure a single sharp exponent, producing smeared, exponent-shifted transport signatures across an extended doping window around x_c.
